Speculative decoding works by having a small draft model propose k tokens at a stretch, which the target model then accepts or rejects via a correction scheme that preserves the target's exact distribution. The acceptance rate α — the fraction of draft tokens the target keeps — directly determines throughput: if α drops, you're paying draft model cost plus target verification cost while generating fewer tokens per target forward pass than the theoretical max. The central question is: under what conditions does the draft model's token distribution diverge from the target's, how fast does that divergence accumulate across a speculative window, and what does that do to expected accepted tokens E[k_accepted]?

What experts worry about that beginners miss is the compounding nature of the problem. A beginner sees acceptance rate as a static property of a model pair, measured on some benchmark. An expert knows that α is actually a function of the current decoding context — prompt domain, generation length, sampling temperature, and crucially the trajectory of previously generated tokens. If the draft and target disagree on token 3 of a window, the draft is now conditioning its tokens 4–k on a path the target never would have taken, making those subsequent proposals even worse. This trajectory divergence is especially sharp under distribution shift: when the inference-time domain differs from the joint training distribution of the model pair, systematic biases in the draft model get exposed rather than averaged out.

When draft and target diverge systematically, acceptances become negatively autocorrelated within a window: a rejection at position j means the draft has wandered off a path the target dislikes, making positions j+1 through k nearly certain rejections, so the effective α for those trailing positions is far lower than the marginal α you measured at position 1. The scheme is architecturally appealing but breaks distribution exactness the moment the probe's accept/reject decision gates whether the full target runs — because now the joint acceptance probability is p(full verification runs) × p(target accepts | full verification runs), and if the probe has any false-negative rate (rejecting tokens the target would have accepted), you've introduced a systematic bias that no downstream correction scheme can fix without knowing the probe's error rate exactly. This is the critical distinction: in standard speculative decoding, the rejection sampling correction works because the target always runs on every drafted token and the correction is computed from exact target logits; the moment you make the target's execution conditional on an approximate signal, you've left the regime where the correction theorem applies. Medusa's tree-attention verification and Eagle-2's pruning avoid this by still running the full target forward pass over all surviving branches — pruning happens in the draft tree structure, not in whether the target verifies. A scheme that maintained exactness would need to treat probe rejections probabilistically: run the full target anyway with probability ε even when the probe says reject, and use importance weighting to correct — this is essentially a Monte Carlo estimator of the target distribution, and at low ε it recovers most of the compute savings while bounding the distributional error, but the variance of that estimator grows as ε shrinks, meaning you need careful calibration to avoid both bias and high-variance generation. In practice, deployed systems that use probe-like signals (e.g., SpecInfer's draft tree scoring) treat them as ranking mechanisms to allocate verification budget across candidate sequences rather than hard gates, which sidesteps the exactness problem by ensuring the target still touches every candidate — just with different computational priority.

Speculative Rejection (Liao et al., 2024) moves in this direction by framing acceptance as a sequence-level hypothesis test — rather than correcting token by token, it evaluates whether the entire drafted window is plausible under the target by computing a sequence-level likelihood ratio, which is tighter than the product of per-token ratios when consecutive tokens are correlated under the target. A second approach borrows from statistical hypothesis testing: you treat the draft sequence as a sample and test whether it falls in a high-probability region of the target distribution using a concentration inequality — Hoeffding or Bernstein bounds on the log-likelihood ratio give you a sequence-level rejection threshold that accounts for length and variance, not just pointwise error. The practical tightness gain is real but modest: because language distributions have high entropy and long-range dependencies, even sequence-level KL bounds tend to grow with T, just sublinearly rather than linearly under favorable correlation structure — empirically this might mean a 1000-token sequence has 3-4× tighter effective error bounds than the per-token product would predict, not 10-100×. The deeper issue is that all these criteria still require computing target probabilities over the full sequence to evaluate the bound, which partially defeats the compute savings — the useful regime is when you can estimate sequence-level plausibility from partial target evaluations, which remains an open problem with no clean solution as of mid-2025.
